questions.stem: How is a three-figure bearing measured?

options.text: From the nearer of the north or south line

questions.explanation: Every bearing is measured from north, turning clockwise, and written with three figures. That is why east is 090° and west is 270°. The three-figure form means a small angle such as 7° is written 007°.

distractorRationale.b: Turning anticlockwise would make east 270°, which contradicts the compass
distractorRationale.c: Bearings never start from east; the reference line is always north
distractorRationale.d: That describes the older N30°E style of writing directions, not a three-figure bearing

questions.stem: The bearing of Q from P is $070°$. What is the bearing of P from Q?
questions.explanation: The back bearing points the opposite way, so it differs by 180°. Since 070° is less than 180°, add: $070° + 180° = 250°$. A quick sanity check — Q is roughly north-east of P, so P must be roughly south-west of Q, and 250° is indeed close to south-west.

distractorRationale.c: Subtracted from 360°, which reflects the direction in the north line rather than reversing it
distractorRationale.d: A direction and its reverse can never have the same bearing

questions.stem: The bearing of B from A is $210°$. Find the bearing of A from B.
questions.explanation: Because 210° is already more than 180°, subtract: $210° - 180° = 30°$, written as $030°$. The leading zero is part of the answer.

distractorRationale.b: Subtracted from 360°, which does not reverse a direction
distractorRationale.c: Added 30° instead of working with the 180° difference
distractorRationale.d: Added 180° when the bearing was already above 180°; a bearing can never exceed 360°

questions.stem: Express the direction $S\,30°\,W$ as a three-figure bearing.
questions.explanation: $S\,30°\,W$ means start facing south and turn 30° towards the west. South is 180°, and turning towards west means continuing clockwise, so the bearing is $180° + 30° = 210°$.

distractorRationale.a: Ignored the S and W and just used the 30°, which points north-east instead
distractorRationale.b: Turned 30° from south towards the east, giving $180° - 30°$, the mirror image of the correct direction
distractorRationale.d: Measured the 30° from west (270°) rather than from south

questions.stem: A surveyor walks 5 km due north, then 12 km due east. How far, in kilometres, is she from her starting point? Give a number only.
questions.explanation: The north leg and the east leg are perpendicular, so the journey forms a right-angled triangle with legs 5 km and 12 km. By Pythagoras' theorem the direct distance is $\sqrt{5^2 + 12^2} = \sqrt{25 + 144} = \sqrt{169} = 13$ km. Adding the two distances to get 17 km would be the total walked, not the distance from the start.

questions.stem: A surveyor walks 5 km due north from $P$ to $Q$, then 12 km due east from $Q$ to $R$. What is the bearing of $R$ from $P$, to the nearest degree?
questions.explanation: Draw the north line at $P$. The angle to $R$ has the 12 km east leg opposite it and the 5 km north leg adjacent, so $\tan\theta = \frac{12}{5} = 2.4$ and $\theta \approx 67.4°$. To the nearest degree the bearing is $067°$. It must be between 000° and 090° because $R$ lies north-east of $P$.

distractorRationale.a: Used $\tan^{-1}\frac{5}{12}$, swapping the opposite and adjacent sides
distractorRationale.c: Subtracted 67° from 180°, which would place $R$ south-east of $P$
distractorRationale.d: Measured the 67° anticlockwise from north instead of clockwise

questions.stem: A ship sails 20 km from a harbour on a bearing of $060°$. How far east of the harbour is it, correct to 2 decimal places?
questions.explanation: The bearing angle of 60° is measured from the north line, so the eastward part is the opposite side: east $= 20\sin 60° = 20 \times 0.8660 \approx 17.32$ km. The northward part would be $20\cos 60° = 10$ km.

distractorRationale.a: Used $20\cos 60°$, which gives the distance north rather than east
distractorRationale.c: Assumed the whole 20 km was eastward, which would need a bearing of 090°
distractorRationale.d: Used $20\tan 60°$; the tangent is not used when the hypotenuse is the known side

questions.stem: Town $B$ is 15 km from town $A$ on a bearing of $120°$. How many kilometres south of $A$ is $B$? Give a number only.
questions.explanation: A bearing of 120° has passed 090°, so the journey heads south-east. The angle it makes with the **south** line is $180° - 120° = 60°$. The southward part is therefore $15\cos 60° = 15 \times 0.5 = 7.5$ km. (The eastward part is $15\sin 60° \approx 12.99$ km.) Using $\cos 120°$ directly gives $-7.5$, where the minus sign simply confirms the direction is south.

questions.stem: A man walks 4 km due east from $P$ to $Q$, then 4 km due north from $Q$ to $R$. What is the bearing of $R$ from $P$?
questions.explanation: $R$ is 4 km east and 4 km north of $P$. Equal eastward and northward parts mean $\tan\theta = \frac{4}{4} = 1$, so $\theta = 45°$ and the bearing is $045°$ — exactly north-east, which you can also read straight off a sketch.

distractorRationale.b: Gave the direction of the first leg only, ignoring the walk north
distractorRationale.c: That is south-east; the second leg goes north, not south
distractorRationale.d: That is north-west, obtained by turning anticlockwise instead of clockwise

questions.stem: A ship sails 24 km from $P$ on a bearing of $040°$ to $Q$, then 30 km from $Q$ on a bearing of $100°$ to $R$. Find $|PR|$, correct to 1 decimal place.
questions.explanation: The bearing of $P$ from $Q$ is the back bearing of 040°, that is 220°. At $Q$ the two directions are 220° and 100°, so $\angle PQR = 220° - 100° = 120°$. The cosine rule then gives $|PR|^2 = 24^2 + 30^2 - 2(24)(30)\cos 120° = 576 + 900 + 720 = 2196$, so $|PR| = \sqrt{2196} \approx 46.9$ km. Note that $\cos 120° = -0.5$, so the last term is **added**.

distractorRationale.a: Treated $\cos 120°$ as $+0.5$, subtracting 720 instead of adding it
distractorRationale.b: Used Pythagoras, wrongly assuming the angle at $Q$ is 90°
distractorRationale.d: Added the two distances, which is the total sailed, not the direct distance
